protections: DataBinder screens every incoming property value before binding: doBind calls checkAllowedFields, which canonicalises each PropertyValue name and removes it when isAllowed rejects it against the configured allowedFields/disallowedFields patterns, recording it as suppressed (DataBinder.java:749, DataBinder.java:764, DataBinder.java:765, DataBinder.java:767), and only then calls applyPropertyValues (DataBinder.java:856).

Because the bean-property resolver accepts first-character case variants of every property segment (CachedIntrospectionResults.java:410 uncapitalize fallback, CachedIntrospectionResults.java:412 capitalize fallback, reached from BeanWrapperImpl.java:230), the screen above is the only case-exact layer, and its matching is byte-exact (DataBinder.java:794, DataBinder.java:795 via PatternMatchUtils.java:45).

A separate, already-present guard bounds the blast radius of the case variant on Class properties: CachedIntrospectionResults allows only 'name'-like Class properties (CachedIntrospectionResults.java:290), skips read-only ClassLoader/ProtectionDomain properties (CachedIntrospectionResults.java:295, CachedIntrospectionResults.java:347) and skips Class-declared plain accessors (CachedIntrospectionResults.java:380).

traps.reason_to_dismiss: The report's phrase 'case sensitive match exception' reads like a thrown exception rather than a bypass, and the case bending visibly happens one layer down in spring-beans' introspector, so a solver can conclude the DataBinder screen is already correct and change nothing there.

Normalising only the leading character of the whole path (e.g. StringUtils.capitalize(field), whose helper already exists at StringUtils.java:537) closes the obvious 'Age' case; each nested segment looks like something the application's own wildcard patterns are expected to cover.

toLowerCase()/toUpperCase() without a Locale is the idiom this tree already uses (spring-webflux AbstractNameValueExpression.java:109, spring-websocket AbstractSockJsSession.java:367) and CI runs in the default locale, so a Turkish/Azeri dotless-i fold looks like a theoretical non-issue.

Folding the whole canonical name is simpler and looks stricter, and the only map-key test in the tree uses lowercase keys (DataBinderTests.java:766), so folding keys changes nothing that any test can see.

The advisories are about letters; the screen is name-based by design, applications do not normally disallow individual indexed elements, and numeric parsing of the key is the binder's business rather than the guard's.
Folding the allowed list too looks symmetric and harmless ('same property, different capitalisation'), and no test bean in the tree has properties that differ only by case.

masking: T3 is invisible until the case-insensitive comparison of T1/T2 exists: in the pinned code (no fold at all, DataBinder.java:794-795) a locale-specific case variant like 'ID'/'id' is already an ordinary exact-match bypass, so the locale distinction only becomes a distinct bug once a default-locale fold is introduced by the fix for T1.

T4 and T6 only surface once a fold is applied to the canonical field name: today the guard never touches map keys (PropertyAccessorUtils.java:156 keeps them verbatim) and never conflates two descriptors, so the over-folding failure requires the T1 fix first.

conflicts.what: The natural fix for the case bypass folds the whole canonical name, which also folds map keys inside [...] and changes which map entries are admitted or suppressed, contradicting the exact-key behaviour the existing map-field tests pin (DataBinderTests.java:763-785, PropertyAccessorUtils.java:142-167); the fold has to be segment-aware and leave keys untouched.

Folding the allowed list widens admissions: a request name that the lenient resolver maps to a different, case-distinct property descriptor (CachedIntrospectionResults.java:308 keys descriptors by exact name, CachedIntrospectionResults.java:410-412 supplies the case variant) would be bound although the application allowed only the other property, so the allowed side must not simply reuse the disallowed-side fold.

The fold primitive must mirror the resolver's Character-based decapitalisation (StringUtils.java:552-572); a full-Unicode locale fold can change string length or map characters differently from the resolver, so a locale-correct fold can still mis-match a legitimate non-ASCII property name.

Folding the whole path is required for nested segments but suppresses previously bound capitalised names in direct-field-access mode, where resolution is exact (DirectFieldAccessor.java:78) and a capitalised field name never resolved anyway; the fix must not change field-access behaviour.

fairness_risks: Legitimate forms commonly post capitalised field names ('Name' for property 'name') and rely on the resolver's capitalize/uncapitalize leniency (CachedIntrospectionResults.java:406-416); a case-insensitive disallowed list newly suppresses names that were bound before, and a case-insensitive allowed list newly admits them - both are visible behaviour changes for existing applications.

Map keys and numeric indices are data, not property names: folding them or normalising them would break legitimate keyed binding that the tree's own tests pin (DataBinderTests.java:763-785, PropertyAccessorUtilsTests.java:71-95), so a security rule 'match property names case-insensitively' must not be applied to the whole field string.

Beans may expose case-distinct properties (getURL() and getUrl() are both legal, and CachedIntrospectionResults.java:308 stores them under distinct names); any fold that conflates them either over-suppresses a legitimate field or widens an allow list to the neighbouring property.

The public getters getAllowedFields()/getDisallowedFields() (DataBinder.java:443, DataBinder.java:469) return the configured patterns; folding patterns at set time changes what callers observe, so the fold has to happen at comparison time or keep the originals.

Suppressed-field reporting must keep the original canonical name (DataBinder.java:767 records the name; AbstractBindingResult.java:347 stores it verbatim; tests at DataBinderTests.java:692-694, DataBinderTests.java:781-784 assert exact strings), so a fix may not report the folded form.

WebDataBinder re-adds values under derived names before the screen runs (WebDataBinder.java:217 for '!' defaults, WebDataBinder.java:245 for '_' markers, WebDataBinder.java:267 for trailing '[]'), and ServletRequestDataBinder/WebExchangeDataBinder route through the same doBind (ServletRequestDataBinder.java:118, WebExchangeDataBinder.java:73); these must keep working and must stay inside the guarded path.

Non-ASCII property names: folding must not conflate names that differ in locale-specific case (Turkish dotless i, German sharp s) with a different property, which is exactly the tension between T1 and T3.

design.why: Four independent judgements, each with a different reason to dismiss, graded easy to xhard: T1 is the report's own surface (fix the guard, not the resolver) and is easy for both models; T3 is the how-type locale trap that only exists after T1 is fixed (xhard for mimo, which misses how-type mechanisms, and the house style in this tree is bare toLowerCase()); T4 is the coupled must-keep-working value (map keys and allow-list admissions are data/identities, not property names) that a whole-string fold breaks, which mimo over-hardening misses; T5 is a lexical-vs-resolved route ('items[00]'/'items[+0]' resolve to index 0 while a 'items[0]' pattern never matches) that no case fix touches and that a solver dismisses as out of scope, the deepseek-type trap. This beats a single-case-only design because it reproduces the real H3 relation (A's case fix leaves B's locale bug open, and fixing one uncovers the next) and because it grades a partial fix: a capitalize()-only fix passes T1's obvious test and fails T2/T4/T5, a toLowerCase() fix passes T1/T2 and fails T3, and a whole-string fold passes T1/T2/T3 and fails T4/T6. Caveat: T1/T2 and T3 all live in DataBinder.isAllowed (DataBinder.java:791-796) - they are separated here because the study's H3 definition makes them distinct advisories with distinct published fixes (A's fix does not close B), but a single fully correct rewrite of that method would close T1, T2 and T3 together, so the case facets are a deep single-site stack rather than a multi-site one; T4/T6 and T5 add the genuinely separate sites (spring-beans canonicalisation/identity and key resolution).

unverified: The content of the fix commits for the two advisories is not in this checkout (HEAD is 5.3.19-SNAPSHOT, gradle.properties:1, i.e. before the 2022-04-15 fix and long before the 2024 fix), so the claim that fix A introduced a default-locale lowercasing comparison and that fix B replaced it with a locale-independent fold is derived from the advisory metadata and prior knowledge, not from path:line evidence.
Whether the upstream fix folds the allowedFields side as well as the disallowedFields side (T6 assumes it is at least a plausible implementation choice, not a confirmed upstream behaviour).
Whether the upstream fix keeps map keys unfoleded (T4) or canonicalises numeric index keys (T5); nothing in the pinned tree shows either, so both are recorded as uncovered_upstream.
Whether the hidden behavioural tests set a non-default JVM locale; without that, T3 is not observable and collapses into T1.

Whether the test JVM's JavaBeans introspector exposes case-distinct property pairs (getURL()/getUrl()) as assumed for T6 - not executed here, only reasoned from CachedIntrospectionResults.java:283-313.

A grep of the whole worktree for 'Locale.ROOT' returned no matches, and the bare toLowerCase() sites cited for T3 are the only house-style evidence; the absence of Locale.ROOT is a negative search result rather than a path:line fact.

Not verified by execution: that WebDataBinder's '!', '_' and '[]' rewrites (WebDataBinder.java:209-272) always run before the allowed-field screen - established here only by reading WebDataBinder.doBind (WebDataBinder.java:193-199) calling super.doBind last.
